blocks.text: After naming Babylon as its target, the oracle moves from the mustering of an army, through the terror of the day of Jehovah, to flight, slaughter, and Babylon’s lasting desolation. This belongs to a body of prophetic oracles that responds to imperial aggression and addresses the moral order of the nations.

The prophets use “the day of Jehovah” amid national crisis to warn of covenant judgment and to promise future vindication. In this chapter the phrase introduces the collapse of human strength, the punishment of pride and wickedness, and upheaval described on a cosmic scale.

The chapter’s poetic oracle belongs to prophetic speech shaped by covenant lawsuit, royal courts, temple worship, and the pressures associated with major empires. Royal “day of the king” imagery also helps explain the expression “day of Jehovah,” but Isaiah presents Jehovah himself—not a human ruler—as the judge and deliverer who commands the forces of judgment.

One practical reading map treats Isaiah 1–12 and 13–27 as successive major divisions, making chapter 13 the beginning of a new reading segment. This outline is an organizational aid, not proof of six authors or of one uncontested structure for the whole book.

Across Isaiah, judgment addresses Judah, Israel, and foreign nations. Empires may serve as instruments within the book’s portrayal of events, yet they remain accountable themselves. Isaiah also looks beyond judgment toward nations learning, worshiping, and sharing in restoration.
